correctness.rationale: For each of the five allowed pair types the proof exhibits a potential with exactly the selected two root maximizers, and for each excluded pair an alternative exact root-sum decomposition. The origin-deletion threshold follows by sign of the unique possible exposing maximum for composable arcs. Dimension, counts, all degrees, diameter, and simple vertices are derived algebraically. The executable integer checker reports success on all 125 triples with part sizes 1..5, 3375 vertex instances and 24975 predicted edges. The proof, not enumeration, supports all positive integers.

evidence: Setiabrata 2020 studies all acyclic root polytopes WITH origin; the relevant theorem is exact for that larger polytope. Numata et al. cover facets of any directed edge polytope. The full-tournament record classifies all pairs in the graph with internal layer arcs as well.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The general facet theorem is a framework from which this concrete edge census could be derived through further analysis, but it is not a ready-made implication of its printed local statements. The full-tournament one-skeleton result is not a stronger parameter instance: removing within-layer root vertices can create edges, so induced-graph restriction is invalid. The new claim includes precisely which edges appear upon origin deletion, absent from the origin-adjoined results.

evidence: The transitive-tournament formula has n-2 new edges after origin removal, versus ac new edges here when b=1. In Setiabrata 2020, the origin is a vertex in the studied root polytope, while the candidate distinguishes its removal. Numata et al. do not state the particular three-layer graph/degree criterion.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The difference between models is structural, not terminological: same-root adjacency of the origin-adjoined and nonadjoined versions is not generally equal, and the candidate computes exactly when equality holds. The fully ordered tournament is not the same graph or a parameter specialization of complete three-layer orientation with no internal arcs.

evidence: Setiabrata, arXiv:2001.05191, Theorems 3.4 and 3.18, classify faces after adjoining the origin; Numata–Takahashi–Tamaki, arXiv:2203.14521, Theorems 1.1–1.3, give general dimension/facet criteria.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: A root polytope of a transitively oriented complete three-layer graph is an acyclic directed edge polytope. Neither cited classification states the full graph of the version omitting the origin. The extra composable edges for a singleton middle layer have negative support and do not survive in the origin-adjoined face lattice.

originality.rationale: The focused published-record queries did not find a matching three-layer adjacency or origin-deletion threshold. Full relevant mathematical statements were compared: existing general face criteria characterize other aspects of the polytope (notably the origin-adjoined version) and an explicit full-tournament one-skeleton has a genuinely different arc set and deletion behavior. The complete concrete classification plus quadratic edge birth is not stated in inspected sources. Strong general face theorems and unindexed specializations remain an acknowledged priority risk.
residual_risks: Setiabrata general face machinery may yield part of the explicit result by specialization, although it does not itself state the non-origin-adjoined graph or its sharp origin-deletion threshold.
An older unindexed or differently titled exact tripartite graph result may exist.
No independent scholarly priority review has been performed.

value.rationale: A complete three-layer orientation is the smallest transitively closed non-graded layered family, while two layers yield only products of simplices. Its root polytope acquires an exact degree and simplicity spectrum and a sharp origin-deletion transition: ac new edges at a singleton middle, none for all larger middle layers. This naturally compares two standard root-polytope constructions and is meaningful for arbitrarily large outer parts, not a finite lookup.
